summary: Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered web dashboard, live at www.flamesphere.earth. It turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insights for spacecraft, space stations and Moon and Mars habitats. We brought 25 PSI combustion investigations, with 2,009 test rows, 364 publications and 52 study documents, into one database that can be searched as a whole. A chat agent answers questions such as "Which studies cover a Moon-habitat atmosphere?" by calling tools that filter, rank and chart this data. Every number comes from the data and cites its PSI ID and DOI, never from the model's memory. The dashboard ranks investigations by how relevant they are to crew habitats. It shows which studies cover the expected lunar habitat air (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less) and compares studies side by side. It links the Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and Mir fires to the research on each hazard, and it shows where data is missing: PSI has no partial-gravity combustion results yet. Moon habitats will use air that burns more easily than Earth's. Engineers, researchers and students need this scattered evidence in one place they can trust and check
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard, live at www.flamesphere.earth. It helps people explore NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion data and get fire-safety insights for spacecraft, space stations and Moon and Mars habitats. You can ask a question in plain language, or use the normal filters, buttons and the ⌘K command menu. A chat agent reads the question and picks a tool. The tool runs ordinary code on our prepared database and returns structured results with citations. The app shows those results as a chart or panel beside the chat, and the agent explains them briefly. Every number cites its PSI investigation ID and DOI. When the data doesn't hold an answer, the app says so instead of guessing.

The main views are:

- investigations ranked by fire-safety relevance to crew habitats, with the reasons for each rank

- a Moon-habitat atmosphere map showing which studies cover the expected lunar habitat air (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less)

- side-by-side comparison of 2–3 studies

- case-study cards linking the Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and Mir fires to the research on each hazard

- a gaps view: PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet, so microgravity and normal-gravity results set the bounds for lunar gravity

- Earth applications

Behind the app, a data pipeline does the heavy work once, ahead of time. It pulls 25 combustion investigations from the PSI API and downloads their data tables and documents. It cleans and joins the tables. AI then extracts test conditions, summaries and relevance scores, and each extracted value must quote its source text or it is rejected. Finally the pipeline loads everything into a database and a search index. An automated audit then checks the result against NASA's site: all 25 records match live PSI, all 25 DOIs resolve, and 0 of 24,408 table cells were lost.

Benefits

- It brings 25 investigations, 2,009 test rows, 364 publications and 52 study documents into one place you can search.

- A question that used to mean reading many tables, PDFs and spreadsheets now takes seconds. The first chart appears in about 2 seconds (median).

- Every claim can be checked: each one links to its NASA source, and fields written by AI are labelled "AI-generated, see source".

Intended impact

The app helps engineers, researchers, professors and students choose habitat atmospheres, materials, and fire detection and suppression equipment for lunar and Martian missions. It also points out where research is missing, such as partial-gravity combustion, which helps decide which upcoming experiments matter most. Finally, it connects the space findings to Earth uses such as water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors and firefighter gear.

Tools, languages and software

- Languages: Python and TypeScript.

- Backend: FastAPI, with streamed chat responses. SQLite with full-text search. A Chroma vector index using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.

- Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Apache ECharts, cmdk and Zustand.

- AI: GLM 5.3 Flash on Fireworks AI runs the live agent. Anthropic Sonnet 5.5 was used to do one-time extraction, summaries and scoring.

- Data: NASA PSI (CC0-1.0), cited by DOI.

What is creative

- The agent builds the screen, not just a text reply. Each answer arrives as charts and panels you can explore further.

- Charts are made from data and a chart type the agent chooses, drawn by a fixed set of components. The agent never writes chart code, so charts stay reliable.

- We treat missing data as a finding: the gaps view shows clearly what NASA hasn't tested yet.

- Historic spacecraft fires are linked directly to the experiments that study each hazard.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: the agent never states numbers from memory, and we tested it on our six suggested prompts (24/24 turns passed).

- No dead ends: every view also works through filters and buttons, so a wrong agent answer never blocks the user.

- Licensing: we followed PSI's licence and citation rules.

- Speed and cost: we chose a fast, low-cost model.

- Security: API keys are never stored in the code.

- Audience: the app is designed for researchers and students.

- Gravity gap: lunar gravity has no direct data yet, so we show bounds instead of overstating what is known.
